inline.s: This holy Dharma (all dharmas are without self-nature, empty and without anything existing) can subdue Mara, subdue afflictions, subdue the five aggregates, subdue the twelve sense-spheres, subdue the eighteen elements; it subdues those who assert the existence of the five aggregates, those who assert the existence of the twelve sense-spheres; it subdues those who assert the existence of the eighteen elements, those who assert the existence of sentient beings, of persons, of a soul, of a life, of existence, of non-existence — subduing all who follow wrong practices. Sariputra, this holy Dharma of mine can subdue all clinging and grasping, even down to those who assert the existence of dharmas, who do not rejoice in the true characteristics of all dharmas, and who go against the Buddha's Dharma.

[Five aggregates] That is, the five skandhas: form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. [Twelve sense-spheres] The six sense organs and the six sense objects. [Eighteen elements] The six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the six consciousnesses. [Soul] Within dharmas such as the five aggregates this refers to falsely reckoning that there is a self, with the life faculty fully established and sustained without interruption; this is one of the sixteen types of self conjured up by non-Buddhist teachers. [This holy Dharma of mine] This refers to “all dharmas are without self-nature, empty and without anything existing.”

Why is this so? Sariputra, if there are sentient beings who speak of self, speak of persons, speak of sentient beings, speak of annihilation, speak of permanence, speak of existence, speak of non-existence, speak of dharmas, speak of provisional names, speak of extremes — all such go against the Buddha and dispute with the Buddha. Sariputra, even those who attain a little of the Dharma dispute with the Buddha. Those who dispute with the Buddha all enter wrong paths and are not my disciples. If they are not my disciples, then they dispute with nirvana, dispute with the Buddha, dispute with the Dharma, dispute with the Sangha.

Why is this so? Sariputra, because if there are sentient beings who speak of self, speak of persons, speak of sentient beings, speak of annihilation, speak of permanence, speak of existence, speak of non-existence, speak of dharmas, speak of provisional names, speak of extremes — all of these go against the Buddha and dispute with the Buddha. Sariputra, even those who calculate and cling to a little attainment of the Dharma are likewise disputing with the Buddha. Those who dispute with the Buddha all enter wrong paths and are not my disciples. If they are not my disciples, then they dispute with nirvana, dispute with the Buddha, dispute with the Dharma, dispute with the Sangha.

All dharmas are ultimately empty, without anything existing, beyond attainment. Therefore, the various views that contradict this holy Dharma are all wrong views that oppose the Buddha, oppose the Dharma, and oppose the Sangha; those who hold wrong views are not disciples of the Buddha.

[Provisional name] A false name. All dharmas originally have no name; it is people who impose a provisional name upon them. [Those who speak of extremes] Those who assert the view of extremes. [View of extremes] A wrong view that leans to one side. For example, some people stubbornly hold that after death there is annihilation and no future life — this is called the "view of annihilation" or the "view of non-existence"; others stubbornly hold that after death one remains human, and that after death pigs, horses, oxen, and sheep are still pigs, horses, oxen, and sheep — this is called the "view of permanence" or the "view of existence." These views that cling to annihilation or to permanence all lean to one side and do not accord with the Middle Way, hence the name "view of extremes." [Those who attain a little of the Dharma] Those who calculate and cling to a little attainment of the Dharma.

Sariputra, for persons with such views, I do not permit them to leave home and receive the precepts. Sariputra, for persons with such views, I do not permit them to accept so much as a single drink of water for their own sustenance.

Sariputra, for persons with such wrong views, I do not permit them to leave home and receive the precepts. Sariputra, for persons with such wrong views, I do not permit them to accept the offering of even a single drink of water.

Sariputra, if a person renounces and abandons such unwholesome clinging and grasping, and leaves home to seek the Way within my Dharma — not thinking of nirvana, not taking nirvana as an object of thought, not clinging to nirvana, and without fright or fear toward the Dharma of ultimate emptiness — this person, for the sake of severing dharmas alone, diligently practices with vigor; how much the more so regarding such unwholesome clinging as clinging to self, clinging to sentient beings, clinging to persons, clinging to dharmas. For the sake of severing all clinging, this person diligently cultivates only the signless samadhi, and in the signless samadhi also does not grasp a sign. This person realizes: the characteristics of all dharmas are a single characteristic — what is called the signless.

Sariputra, if a person severs and abandons these unwholesome clingings, leaves home within my Dharma to seek the Way, does not think of nirvana, does not take nirvana as an object of thought, does not cling to nirvana, and is without fright or fear toward this holy Dharma of ultimate emptiness — for the sake of severing attachment to dharmas this person diligently practices with vigor; how much less would they falsely cling to a self, to persons, to sentient beings, and to the Way of Dharma as real? For the sake of severing all clinging, these people single-mindedly and diligently cultivate the signless samadhi, and in the signless samadhi also do not grasp it as real (the signless samadhi is to cultivate illusion by means of illusion; when the illusion is exhausted, the dream awakens). They realize that the characteristics of all dharmas are in fact a single characteristic,
and this “characteristic” is itself nothing
[Persons with such views] People with the wrong views described above. [Do not permit] Not allowed; the word “listen” here carries the sense of “permit.”

Sariputra, this is what is called the compliant acceptance of the Dharma within the holy Dharma. One who attains this compliant acceptance of the Dharma is then called my disciple — able to consume offerings, not in vain receiving this body.

Sariputra, these people who “diligently cultivate the signless samadhi, and in the signless samadhi do not grasp a sign” and who “realize that the characteristics of all dharmas are a single characteristic, that is, the signless” — these are called those who attain the compliant acceptance of the Dharma within the holy Dharma. One who attains this compliant acceptance is then truly my disciple, able to receive offerings and not betray this exceedingly rare human body.

[Compliant acceptance of the Dharma] That is, compliant forbearance, one of the four kinds of forbearance. [The four kinds of forbearance] Subjugation-forbearance, compliant-forbearance, non-arising-forbearance, and serene-extinction-forbearance. Subjugation-forbearance: for a beginner practitioner, in order to endure and comply with adverse circumstances, one must first subdue and pacify one's own mind. Compliant-forbearance: after the mind has been pacified for a long time, when encountering situations and conditions one naturally endures without needing to force restraint; at this point the mind is gentle, pliant, and compliant. Non-arising-forbearance: for a person in the stage of Sagehood, one realizes that all dharmas originally do not arise; whether sentient or non-sentient, all are dependently arisen and without self-nature, and in their very substance are empty; therefore, within the nature that is without self-nature, the mind of forbearance is unmoved and one personally realizes non-arising. Serene-extinction-forbearance: for a Sage at the stage of fruition, one fully realizes the realm of nirvana's serene extinction; both the characteristic of motion and of stillness accord with Thusness.

[Not in vain receiving this body] Not in vain receiving a human body (not betraying this exceedingly rare human body). Among the six realms, the human realm is the most suitable for cultivating and studying the Buddha-Dharma. Yet to obtain a human body is extremely difficult. The Buddhist scriptures contain three parables concerning "the difficulty of obtaining a human body." The Agama Sutra says: "The human body is hard to obtain, like a blind turtle surfacing within the hole of a floating log; such a matter is exceedingly difficult." The Trapusa Sutra says: "Suppose there is a person atop Mount Sumeru who lets down a fine thread, and below another person holds a needle to meet it, while in between a fierce whirlwind blows, so that the thread is hard to enter the needle's eye. Obtaining a human body is harder still." The Nirvana Sutra says: "Obtaining a human body is like the dust upon one's fingernail; losing a human body is like the dust of the great earth." The human body is hard to obtain and is now obtained; the Buddha-Dharma is hard to hear and is now heard; if this body is not delivered in this very life, then in what life shall it be delivered? [Dust upon the fingernail] Also written as dust upon the nail; that is, the soil upon a fingernail (the nail of the finger).

Why is this so? Sariputra, I am the Dharma of true characteristics. It cannot be entered, cannot be grasped, cannot be abandoned, cannot be clung to, cannot be spoken, and severs the path of words. Without joy, without delight, severing the mind of craving and delight; not produced by a confluence of conditions, apart from all causes and conditions; without a path, severing the path, up to without any path; severing all words, discussions, and sounds; without form, without color, without grasping, without attachment, without function; without real, without false, without darkness, without brightness; without destruction, without dispute, without union, without scattering; without motion, without thought, without discrimination. It cannot be shown; not defiled, not pure, not name, not characteristic, not a mental factor, not something the mind can comprehend.

Why is this so? Sariputra, what I speak is the Dharma of true characteristics — all dharmas are without self-nature, empty and without anything existing. It cannot be entered, cannot be grasped, cannot be abandoned, cannot be clung to, cannot be spoken, and severs the path of words. Without joy, without delight, severing the mind of craving and delight; not produced by a confluence of conditions, apart from all causes and conditions; without a path, without a severed path, up to without any path; severing all words, discussions, and sounds; without form, without color, without grasping, without attachment, without function; without real, without false, without darkness, without brightness; without destruction, without dispute, without union, without scattering; without motion, without thought, without discrimination. It cannot be shown; not defiled, not pure, not name, not characteristic, not a mental factor, not something the mind can comprehend.

Here the Blessed One again uses many instances of "not," "without," and "non-" to further clarify the principle of the true characteristics of all dharmas (the Dharma of true characteristics) that "originally there is not a single thing" — all dharmas are ultimately empty, without anything existing, beyond attainment. Such passages recur many times in the scripture that follows.

[I am the Dharma of true characteristics] What I speak is the Dharma of true characteristics — all dharmas are without self-nature, empty and without anything existing. [Without a path, severing the path, up to without any path] Without a path, without a severed path, up to without any path. Here "path" refers to the teachings of the Dharma. [Mental factors] That is, the dharmas belonging to mind — the various mental phenomena belonging to mind; altogether there are fifty-one such dharmas (fifty-one categories). [Not something the mind can comprehend] True characteristics are not an object, hence they are not something the mind can comprehend.

Within my Dharma there is no male and no female, no deva and no naga, no yaksa, no gandharva, no kumbhanda, no pisaca; no annihilation, no permanence; no self, no sentient being, no person; no coming, no going; no emergence, no entry; no precept, no transgression; no purity, no defilement; no samadhi, no concentration, no faculty of concentration; no dhyana, no faculty of dhyana; no knowledge, no seeing; no greed, no dispute; no path, no fruit of the path; no wisdom, no faculty of wisdom; no enlightenment, no non-enlightenment; no liberation, no non-liberation; no fruit, no attainment of fruit; no power, no non-power; no fearlessness, no non-fearlessness; no thought, no faculty of thought; no sitting, no walking, no dignified deportment; no this, no that; no recollection and discrimination; no bodhi, no limbs of bodhi; no wisdom, no non-wisdom; no earth, no water, no fire, no wind; no offense, no merit; no dharma, no non-dharma; no suffering, no bliss. It uproots the very basis of all idle speculation, forever leaving all behind — cold and without smoke.

Within this holy Dharma of mine there is no male and no female, no assembly of devas and no assembly of nagas, no yaksa, no gandharva, no kumbhanda, no pisaca; no annihilation, no permanence; no self, no person, no sentient being; no coming, no going; no emergence, no entry; no precept, no transgression; no purity, no defilement; no samadhi, no concentration, no faculty of concentration; no dhyana, no faculty of dhyana; no knowledge, no seeing; no greed, no dispute; no path, no fruit of the path; no wisdom, no faculty of wisdom; no enlightenment, no non-enlightenment; no liberation, no non-liberation; no fruit, no attainment of fruit; no power, no non-power; no fearlessness, no non-fearlessness; no thought, no faculty of thought; no sitting, no walking, no dignified deportment; no this, no that; no recollection and discrimination; no bodhi, no limbs of bodhi; no wisdom, no non-wisdom; no earth, no water, no fire, no wind; no offense, no merit; no dharma, no non-dharma; no suffering, no bliss. It uproots the very basis of all idle speculation, forever leaving all behind — cold and without smoke.

[Within my Dharma] The "Dharma" here refers to the holy Dharma described earlier, "all dharmas are without self-nature, empty and without anything existing." [No deva, no naga] There is no assembly of devas and also no assembly of nagas. [Yaksa, gandharva, kumbhanda, pisaca] These all belong to the eight classes of ghostly hosts led by the four heavenly kings. The eight classes of ghostly hosts are: one, gandharvas (fragrance-eating ghosts); two, pisacas (mad ghosts); three, kumbhandas (life-energy-devouring ghosts); four, pretas (hungry ghosts); five, the various nagas; six, putanas (stinking hungry ghosts); seven, yaksas (brave and strong ghosts); eight, raksasas (swift ghosts). [The four heavenly kings] The heavenly king of the east who upholds the realm, the heavenly king of the south who increases growth, the heavenly king of the west of wide eyes, and the heavenly king of the north who hears much. [Faculty of concentration] Concentration can give rise to all merits and virtues, therefore it is called a faculty; it is one of the five faculties. [The five faculties] The faculty of faith, the faculty of vigor, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. Because these five dharmas are the root that gives rise to the holy path, they are therefore called the "five faculties." [Limbs of bodhi] That is, the seven limbs of bodhi — the seven kinds of awakening revealed by the five faculties and five powers: one, the limb of bodhi of choosing the Dharma — discerning true from false dharmas by wisdom; two, the limb of bodhi of vigor — with a courageous heart diligently practicing the true Dharma; three, the limb of bodhi of joy — the mind attaining the good Dharma and giving rise to joy; four, the limb of bodhi of ease — removing the gross defilements of body and mind and attaining lightness and ease; five, the limb of bodhi of mindfulness — constantly contemplating the true Dharma so that concentration and wisdom are balanced; six, the limb of bodhi of concentration — the mind fixed on a single object without scattering; seven, the limb of bodhi of equanimity — abandoning all false dharmas and diligently practicing the true Dharma. [The five powers] The five kinds of power arising from the firm establishment of the five faculties: the power of faith, the power of vigor, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. [Cold and without smoke] Like a fire completely extinguished, cooled, and its smoke gone as well; this is a metaphor for an extremely complete separation.

Sariputra, to state the essentials: my Dharma entirely breaks all thoughts, all views, all bonds, all arrogant conceits; it does not think of all that is recollected, and removes and severs all manner of speech. Within my Dharma there is no impermanence and no non-impermanence, no suffering and no bliss, no defilement and no purity, no annihilation and no permanence, no self, no sentient being, no person, no soul, no life, no birth and no cessation.

Sariputra, to state the essentials: this holy Dharma of mine entirely breaks all thoughts, all views, all desires, all arrogant conceits; it does not think of all that is recollected, and removes and severs all manner of speech. Within this holy Dharma of mine there is no impermanence and no non-impermanence, no suffering and no bliss, no defilement and no purity, no annihilation and no permanence, no self, no person, no sentient being, no soul, no life, no birth and no cessation.

[Bonds] All desires. "Bond" means what binds and ties; here it refers to "desire." Desire is the root of afflictions, binding the cultivator of the Way so that he cannot gain liberation and sinks in birth and death. In the Sutra of the Buddha's Teaching of the Forty-Two Chapters, the Buddha says: "That which makes people foolish and deluded is love and desire." "He who practices the Way is like one carrying dry grass; when fire comes he must avoid it; when the practitioner sees desire he must certainly keep far from it." "He who practices the Way is like an ox bearing a heavy load walking through deep mud; exhausted, he does not dare to look left or right, and only when he emerges from the mud can he rest. The renunciant should regard lust and desire as worse than mud, and with a straightforward mind think of the Way, and so escape suffering." [Arrogant conceit] To speak of attaining a superior Dharma and so give rise to a conceited mind. For example, not yet having attained the holy path, one claims to have attained it. The Lotus Sutra says: "These people have deep and heavy roots of sin, and through arrogant conceit, not having attained they claim to have attained, not having realized they claim to have realized; such are their faults."

Why is this so? Sariputra, the Tathagata in regard to dharmas has no attainment whatsoever, and no cessation — therefore it is called nirvana — and he does not even see one who attains nirvana. Sariputra, the Buddha does not think of nirvana, does not take nirvana as an object of thought, and does not cling to nirvana. Therefore you should know that this is the foremost wonder and rarity! What is called the Tathagata's speaking of all dharmas as without birth and without cessation, without characteristics and without activity, causing people to gain faith and understanding — this is all the more rare and wonderful!

Why is this so? Sariputra, the Tathagata in regard to all dharmas has no attainment whatsoever, and also has no cessation — therefore it is called nirvana — and he does not even see one who attains nirvana. Sariputra, the Buddha does not think of nirvana, does not take nirvana as an object of thought, and does not cling to nirvana. Therefore you should know that this is the foremost wonder and rarity! This is what is called the Tathagata's speaking of all dharmas as without birth and without cessation, without characteristics and without activity, causing people to gain faith and understanding — all the more rare and wonderful!

[Nirvana] Translated into Chinese as "perfect stillness," where "perfect" means perfecting all the virtues of wisdom and "stillness" means extinguishing all delusions and karma. It is also translated as "extinction and transcendence," where "extinction" means extinguishing the three kinds of delusion — views and thoughts, dust-like particles of delusion, and fundamental ignorance — and "transcendence" means going beyond the birth-and-death of delimited forms and the birth-and-death of transformational change. Taken together, when a person's wisdom and virtue have both reached the realm of ultimate perfection, and even birth-and-death and afflictions have been surpassed and put to an end, this is called "nirvana." This is also the realm of Suchness that sages realize — unborn and unceasing, transcending time and space.

blocks.text: 2. The Chapter on Recollecting the Buddha

inline.s: The preceding chapter, "The True Characteristics of All Dharmas," is a general exposition; from here onward, based on the true characteristics of all dharmas, the teaching is given in differentiated detail.
At that time, Sariputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One! Within this Dharma, what is meant by an evil spiritual friend, and what is meant by a good spiritual friend?"
At that time, Sariputra respectfully asked the Buddha: "World-Honored One! Within this holy Dharma, what is an evil spiritual friend, and what is a good spiritual friend?"

The Buddha now replies according to the principle that "the true characteristics of all dharmas are unborn and unceasing, without characteristics and without activity, beyond anything existing, beyond attainment."

The Buddha told Sariputra: "If there is a monk who instructs another monk, saying: 'Monk, you should recollect the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, the precepts, generosity, and the heavens. Monk, you should contemplate the body, taking up this characteristic of the body, namely impurity; you should contemplate that all conditioned dharmas are entirely impermanent, and contemplate that all dharmas are empty, without a self. Monk, you should take up the characteristic of the object of cognition, bind your mind within that object, think only on the characteristic of emptiness, and delight in the good Dharma. You should take up the characteristic of unwholesome dharmas, and having taken up that characteristic of unwholesome dharmas, for the sake of severing them, contemplate and cultivate. That is, to sever greed and desire, contemplate the characteristic of impurity; to sever anger and hatred, contemplate the characteristic of loving-kindness; to sever delusion, contemplate the dharmas of dependent arising. Always recollect the pure precepts and deeply take up the characteristic of emptiness. Diligently practice with vigor, and for the sake of attaining the four dhyanas, single-mindedly seek the Way. Contemplate that unwholesome dharmas are all distress and affliction, and contemplate that the good Dharma is the most secure
(in ancient usage the same as 'stable')

and secure; single-mindedly cultivate the Way, discriminatingly contemplating with true scrutiny. Once the characteristics of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas are truly taken up, contemplate only nirvana as secure and still, and love only nirvana as ultimately pure.' One who teaches thus is called an evil teacher; he maintains it is right teaching, yet it is evil teaching."

The Buddha said to Sariputra: If there is a monk who instructs other monks: "Monk, you should recollect the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, the precepts, generosity, and the heavens (the six recollections). Monk, you should contemplate the body, take up this characteristic of the body, and observe its impurity. You should contemplate that all conditioned dharmas are entirely impermanent, and contemplate that all dharmas are empty, without a self. (On this point the Blessed One criticizes below, saying: "If one calculates a thought of emptiness, this is a thought of self, a thought of sentient beings; emptiness is not to be gained by thought.") Monk, you should take up the characteristic of the object of cognition, bind the mind to it, and think only of the characteristic of emptiness. (Know that the characteristic of objects and conditions is like an illusion, not real; since objects and conditions are not real, to bind the mind to them — is this not false imagining? Hence thinking only on the characteristic of emptiness is in fact clinging to a characteristic of emptiness.) Delight in the good Dharma. (Delighting in the good Dharma is clinging to the characteristic of the good.) Take up the characteristic of unwholesome dharmas. (Taking up the unwholesome is clinging to the characteristic of the unwholesome.) Having taken up the characteristic of unwholesome dharmas, for the sake of severing them, contemplate and cultivate. If it is to sever greed and desire, observe the characteristic of impurity; if it is to sever anger and hatred, observe the characteristic of loving-kindness; if it is to sever delusion, observe the dharmas of dependent arising. (To contemplate and cultivate in order to sever unwholesome dharmas is to pile falsehood upon falsehood; within true characteristics, where is greed and desire, impurity, anger and hatred, loving-kindness, delusion, or dependent arising to be found?) Always recollect the pure precepts and deeply take up the characteristic of emptiness. Diligently practice with vigor, and for the sake of attaining the four dhyanas, single-mindedly seek the Way. Contemplate that unwholesome dharmas are all decay and distress, and contemplate that the good Dharma is most secure and at ease; single-mindedly cultivate the Way, discriminatingly contemplating with true scrutiny. Once the characteristics of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas are truly taken up, contemplate only nirvana as secure and still, and love only nirvana as ultimately pure. (Know that the true characteristics of all dharmas are unborn and unceasing, without characteristics and without activity; within them wholesome and unwholesome dharmas and even nirvana are all beyond attainment. If one says there is a Way to be cultivated and a nirvana to be realized, that person is one of arrogant conceit. Why? Because within true characteristics not a single dharma is to be attained.)" One who teaches thus is called an evil teacher; they take themselves to teach the right teaching, yet in truth it is evil teaching.

[Conditioned dharmas] All things that arise from the union of causes and conditions. [Recollection of the heavens] To recollect that the heavens possess natural happiness, all of it resulting from past diligent practice of the ten wholesome deeds; I too wish to diligently cultivate wholesome karma, and by wholesome causes to obtain wholesome results. [The four dhyanas] The first, second, third, and fourth dhyanas; these are concentration exercises also practiced by ordinary people and non-Buddhist teachers, and by cultivating them one may be reborn in the various heavens of the form realm: the heaven of the first dhyana, the heaven of the second dhyana, the heaven of the third dhyana, and the heaven of the fourth dhyana.

Sariputra, one who teaches thus is called an evil spiritual friend; such a person is called one who slanders me, who aids non-Buddhist teachers, and who also states wrong paths of Dharma for others. Sariputra, for such evil people I do not permit them to accept so much as a single drink of water for their own sustenance. I speak of the teacher, not of the one who receives the teaching. Sariputra, there are many such teachings of arrogant conceit within my Dharma.

Sariputra, one who teaches thus is called an evil spiritual friend; these people slander me and aid non-Buddhist teachers, and also state wrong paths of Dharma for others. Sariputra, for such evil people I do not permit them to accept the offering of even a single drink of water. I am speaking of the teacher, not of the one who receives the teaching. Sariputra, there are many such teachers of arrogant conceit within my Dharma. (These teachers have not obtained the true Dharma, yet take themselves to have obtained it; therefore they are called "arrogant conceit.")
[Arrogant conceit] To speak of having attained a superior Dharma and so give rise to a conceited mind. For example, not yet having attained the holy path, one claims to have attained it.
The above concerns the teacher; the following concerns the one who receives the teaching.

Sariputra, if a recipient of the teaching has received the precepts for five years yet cannot fully abandon that which was thus taught, and within that teaching diligently and earnestly practices; while there are monks who have themselves attained the "without anything existing," he does not go to consult them. I say that such a person, though he has five years, is still called one of wrong views, mingling non-Buddhist Dharma and following the demon's teaching.

Sariputra, if a recipient of the teaching has received the precepts for five years, yet cannot fully abandon such evil teaching (that set of teachings spoken by the teacher above), and within that evil teaching diligently and earnestly practices; although there are monks who have attained the true Dharma of "without anything existing," he does not go to consult and ask them. I say that such a person, though he has five years of ordination, is still called one of wrong views, mingling non-Buddhist Dharma and following the demon's teaching.
[Years of ordination] The number of years since a monk received the full precepts.
The following concerns the recipient of the teaching who is able to reform and repent in time.

Sariputra, if there is a monk who, having received this teaching, upon hearing the Dharma of emptiness and non-attainment, realizes for himself that what he had received before was all wrong views, and toward the Dharma of emptiness and non-attainment has no doubt and no regret, deeply penetrating and attaining it, not relying on any view of self or view of person — Sariputra, I say that such a person is called one who has attained the pure holy life. Sariputra, if there is a monk who accomplishes such a forbearance of non-attainment, though he has not yet reached nirvana without remainder, I predict that this person, in the time of Maitreya Buddha, will be present at the first assembly. At that time, Maitreya Buddha will joyfully proclaim three times: 'This person was able, within the Buddha Dharma of Shakyamuni, to accomplish the forbearance of non-attainment.' Sariputra, whether one who has left home or one who remains at home accomplishes this forbearance, I predict that such a person will surely attain nirvana.

Sariputra, if there is a monk who, having received this evil teaching, upon hearing the Dharma of emptiness and non-attainment, realizes for himself that what he had received before was all wrong views, and toward the Dharma of emptiness and non-attainment has no doubt and no regret, deeply penetrating and attaining it, not relying on any view of self or view of person — Sariputra, I say that such a person is called one who has attained the pure holy life. Sariputra, if there is a monk who accomplishes such a forbearance of non-attainment, though he has not yet now reached nirvana without remainder, I give the prediction that this person, in the time of Maitreya Buddha, will take part in the first assembly. At that time, Maitreya Buddha will joyfully proclaim three times: "This person was able, within the Buddha Dharma of Shakyamuni, to accomplish the forbearance of non-attainment." Sariputra, whether one who has left home or one who remains at home accomplishes this forbearance, I give the prediction that such a person will surely attain nirvana.

[The first assembly] The first assembly of the three assemblies of the dragon-flower tree. [The three assemblies of the dragon-flower tree] In the future, Maitreya Buddha will attain enlightenment beneath the dragon-flower tree in the garden of the Dragon Flower Grove and hold three successive Dharma assemblies. Those who had not attained the Way under the Buddha-Dharma of Shakyamuni in former times will each attain the Way at these assemblies, according to the distinction of superior, middling, and inferior faculties. The Sutra on Maitreya's Descent says: "Maitreya Bodhisattva sits beneath the dragon-flower bodhi tree and attains Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi (becoming a Buddha). In the garden of the Dragon Flower Grove, which is a hundred yojanas across, the great assembly fills it. At the first assembly's discourse, nine hundred sixty million people attain arhatship. At the second great assembly, nine hundred forty million attain arhatship. At the third assembly, nine hundred twenty million attain arhatship." [Nirvana without remainder] When the two delusions of views and thoughts and the body of the five aggregates that one has received are all extinguished, leaving nothing remaining, this is called nirvana without remainder.
The following concerns the recipient of the teaching who is unable to reform and repent.

Sariputra, if a person who has received such teaching, upon hearing the Dharma of emptiness and non-attainment, is immediately alarmed and afraid — such a person is to be pitied, having no one to save him and no one to rely upon, and he goes straight to hell. Why is this so? Sariputra, whoever is alarmed, doubtful, and afraid within the Buddha's teaching — such a person is then complete in the evil paths. Why is that? I constantly say that one who has attainments belongs to the portion of the evil paths.

Sariputra, if a person who has received such evil teaching, upon hearing the Dharma of emptiness and non-attainment, is immediately alarmed and afraid — such a person is to be pitied, having no one to save him and no one to rely upon, and he goes straight to hell. Why is this so? Sariputra, whoever is alarmed, doubtful, and afraid within the Buddha's teaching of true characteristics — such a person is then complete in the evil paths. Why is that? I constantly say that one who has attainments belongs to the portion of the evil paths.

Why is this so? Sariputra, the Dharma attained by the Buddha has no difference. "Is this" and "is not this" — if difference can be established, that is a matter of attainment. Sariputra, a person would rather accomplish the five heinous offenses than accomplish the view of self, the view of sentient beings, the view of persons, the view of a soul, the view of a life, the view of aggregates, sense-spheres, and elements; the clinging to observing precepts and the view of observing precepts; the clinging to samadhi and the view of samadhi; reliance on the thought of the Buddha and attainment of the thought of the Dharma; deciding matters in the Sangha and accomplishing the view of body. Why? Because one who accomplishes the view of body within the Buddha-Dharma is not counted among the Sangha. Sariputra, the assembly of the Buddha's disciples has no discrimination in mind. Sariputra, among the assembly of the Buddha's disciples there is no unwholesome person, no one who breaks the precepts, no one who breaks right views, no one who breaks dignified deportment.

Why is this so? Sariputra, within the Dharma of true characteristics attained by the Buddha there is no difference. "Is this" and "is not this" — if difference can be established, that is a matter of attainment. Sariputra, a person would rather accomplish the five heinous offenses than accomplish the view of self, the view of persons, the view of sentient beings, the view of a soul, the view of a life, the view of aggregates, sense-spheres, and elements; the clinging to observing precepts and the view of observing precepts; the clinging to samadhi and the view of samadhi; reliance on the thought of the Buddha and attainment of the thought of the Dharma; and deciding matters in the Sangha, accomplishing the view of body (while deciding matters in accordance with the precepts within the Sangha, one gives rise to the view of body). Why? Because one who accomplishes the view of body within the Buddha-Dharma is not called a member of the Sangha (not counted among the Sangha). Sariputra, the assembly of the Buddha's disciples has no discrimination in mind. Sariputra, among the assembly of the Buddha's disciples there is no unwholesome person, no one who breaks the precepts, no one who breaks right views ("breaking right views" means destroying right views and giving rise to the sixty-two wrong views), and no one who breaks dignified deportment.

[The five heinous offenses] Five kinds of offenses that utterly go against reason: killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing an arhat, causing blood to flow from a Buddha's body, and breaking the harmony of the Sangha. Because these five are acts of extreme evil, committing any one of them causes one to fall into the uninterrupted hell; hence they are also called "the uninterrupted karma." [View of self] Falsely clinging to the five aggregates, body and mind, as self. [View of persons] Falsely clinging to another's five aggregates, body and mind, as another. [View of sentient beings] Falsely clinging to sentient beings' five aggregates, body and mind, as sentient beings. [View of a soul] Falsely clinging to the lifespan of one's physical body as one's own life. [View of a life] A wrong view that falsely clings to occupation, status, and identity as real. Here "life" refers to the livelihood one depends on to live, that is, one's "occupation." For example, "right livelihood" in the Eightfold Path is a proper occupation. [Aggregates, sense-spheres, and elements] The five aggregates (the five skandhas), the twelve sense-spheres (the six sense organs and six sense objects), and the eighteen elements (the six sense organs, six sense objects, and six consciousnesses). [View of aggregates, sense-spheres, and elements] A wrong view that falsely clings to the five aggregates, the twelve sense-spheres, and the eighteen elements as real. [View of body] A wrong view that falsely clings to the body as real.

Sariputra, what is evil and unwholesome? One who is not counted among the Sangha within the Buddha's assembly is called evil and unwholesome. That is to say, mind and mental factors uniting with various conditions — there is no real thing, yet they merely make discriminations, and because of discrimination they calculate attainment. Such a person's every utterance, with mind following upon mind, even down to wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, is within the holy Dharma called evil and unwholesome.

Sariputra, what is evil and unwholesome? One who is not counted among the Sangha within the Buddha's gate is called evil and unwholesome. Mind and mental factors uniting with various conditions — they are originally not real things, yet they falsely make discriminations, and because of discrimination they calculate attainment. Such people, in every utterance, with mind following upon mind, even down to wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, are within the holy Dharma called evil and unwholesome.
[Mental factors] That is, the dharmas belonging to mind — the various mental phenomena belonging to mind; altogether there are fifty-one such dharmas (fifty-one categories).

Why is this so? Sariputra, in every place of bliss there must be suffering; the Dharma of the Tathagata extinguishes this suffering and bliss. Sariputra, what the Tathagata has attained is within neither desire nor non-desire, neither bliss nor suffering, neither thought nor perception nor cultivation, and even without a thought of emptiness. Why is this so? Sariputra, if one calculates a thought of emptiness, that is a thought of self, a thought of sentient beings, a thought of permanence, a thought of annihilation. Why is this so? Sariputra, following whatever thoughts arise, one then gives rise to many thoughts — all of these fall into wrongness. Sariputra, emptiness means non-thought; this is called emptiness; the thought of emptiness is also empty; this is called emptiness. Sariputra, within emptiness there is no good and no evil, and even no thought of emptiness; therefore it is called emptiness.

Why is this so? Sariputra, in every place of bliss there must be suffering; the Dharma of the Tathagata extinguishes this suffering and bliss. (The Dharma of the Tathagata is ultimately pure, originally without a single thing, hence it extinguishes all suffering and bliss.) Sariputra, what the Tathagata has attained is within neither desire nor absence of desire, neither bliss nor suffering, neither thought nor perception nor cultivation, and even without a thought of emptiness. Why is this so? Sariputra, if one calculates a thought of emptiness, that is a thought of self, a thought of sentient beings, a thought of permanence, a thought of annihilation. Why is this so? Sariputra, following whatever thoughts arise, one then gives rise to many thoughts — all of these fall into wrongness. Sariputra, emptiness means non-thought; this is called emptiness; the thought of emptiness is also empty; this is called emptiness. Sariputra, within emptiness there is no good and no evil, and even no thought of emptiness; therefore it is called emptiness.

Sariputra, the conditioned dharmas can be known and can be understood; emptiness can neither be known nor understood, nor can it be pondered — therefore it is called emptiness. Sariputra, emptiness is not to be gained by thought. Why? Because emptiness is without thought; therefore it is called emptiness. Sariputra, why is it said that one practices the practice of emptiness? Not thinking of any thought whatsoever, and even not thinking of a thought of emptiness — this is called the practice of emptiness. Sariputra, the name of a thought: even when the mind thinks of something, that is called a thought. One who thinks of nothing is then called without thought; because one is apart from all thoughts, it is called without thought. Whatever thought one grasps is a wrong view. Why is this so? Sariputra, to calculate the attainment of still extinction within the holy Dharma all falls into wrong view; how much the more so for speech, and how much the more so for the one who speaks. As for this Dharma of emptiness, what is there to say?

Sariputra, the conditioned dharmas can be known and can be understood, but emptiness can neither be known nor understood nor pondered — therefore it is called emptiness. Sariputra, emptiness is not to be gained by thought (reflection). Why? Because emptiness is without thought; therefore it is called emptiness. Sariputra, why is it also said that one practices the practice of emptiness? Not thinking of any thought whatsoever, and even not thinking of a thought of emptiness — this is called the practice of emptiness. Sariputra, the name of a thought ("name" refers to the designations of things and phenomena): even when the mind thinks of something, that is called a thought (when one thinks of a name, the characteristic of that thing must arise in the mind). One who thinks of nothing is then called without thought; because one is apart from all thoughts, it is called without thought. Whatever thought one grasps is a wrong view. Why is this so? Sariputra, to calculate the attainment of still extinction within the holy Dharma all falls into wrong view; how much the more so for speech, and how much the more so for the one who speaks. As for this Dharma of emptiness, what is there to say?

Sariputra, why do the Buddhas say that all speech is called wrong? It is because those who cannot penetrate all dharmas are all covered over by words; therefore the Tathagata knows that all speech is wrong — so that with even a little speech, one cannot attain the real. Sariputra, the Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi of all Buddhas is entirely without thought and without reflection. Why? The Tathagata in regard to dharmas does not attain their essential nature, nor does he attain thought.

Sariputra, why do the Buddhas say that all speech is called wrong? Because the reason one cannot penetrate the true characteristics of all dharmas is that one is obstructed and covered over by words; therefore the Tathagata knows that all speech is wrong — so that with even a little speech, one cannot attain the true characteristics of all dharmas. Sariputra, the Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi of all Buddhas is entirely without thought and without reflection. Why? The Tathagata in regard to dharmas does not attain their essential nature, nor does he attain thought.
